newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin absent, Russian government faces battles.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin absent, Russian government faces battles.

text.p: Russia's government, still lacking the Kremlin presence of convalescing President Boris Yeltsin, faced bitter battles on several fronts and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told ministers on Thursday to brace for surprises.

Russian news agencies said Chernomyrdin told a cabinet session all ministers had to attend a session of the State Duma lower house of parliament on Friday to defend the 1997 budget, which the communist opposition said on Thursday it would block.
"You must be ready for every possibility. Anything could happen," Itar-Tass quoted Chernomyrdin telling ministers.
The opposition-dominated Duma, which rejected the cabinet's original draft budget, is to discuss a compromise spending plan prepared by a government-parliamentary arbitration commission.
But communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who met Chernomyrdin on Thursday, said afterwards tgat his party, the biggest in the Duma, would not accept the revised budget as it stood.
"We've said it before and I said it today, we will not support this budget," Zyuganov told reporters.
Chernomyrdin told his ministers to defend the plan at the session, admitting that "the situation in the economy is very complicated, especially over payment of wages and pensions".

Zyuganov said he did not rule out that the prime minister could make amendments before Friday that would appease the communists, including sacking some ministers. "Everything depends on what we are presented with tomorrow," Zyuganov said.
He added that his group might agree certain key budget figures to give the government a framework for reworking their plan by the end of the month, when the 1996 budget expires.
Russia has run without a budget in the past. But a conflict between the government and the Duma might lead to Yeltsin having to make a choice between dismissing one or other of the bodies.
Yeltsin, 65, who had a multiple heart bypass operation on November 5, was spending his first day at a country residence where he moved on Wednesday from the nearby Barvikha sanatorium.
The government also faces angry miners, hundreds of thousands of whom began a national strike on Tuesday demanding the government be replaced and that Moscow pay overdue wages.

In the biggest coalmining region, the Kuzbass in southern Siberia, the strike appeared to be losing momentum. Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin, appointed special envoy to the Kuzbass on Wednesday, said he would not go till December 10.
Yet across Russia, Interfax news agency said, the number of mines on strike grew to 132 on Thursday from 124 on Wednesday.
The Duma passed a resolution on Thursday urging Yeltsin to sort out the mines situation and warning it would hold a no- confidence vote if there were no moves to resolve the conflict.
On a brighter note for Chernomyrdin, the Federation Council upper chamber of parliament failed to approve a recommendation to the Duma to stage a no-confidence vote.
Instead, the Council decided to meet in an unscheduled session on December 10 to consider Chernomyrdin's record.
On Wednesday, the normally compliant upper house was in uproar against the prime minister after Chernomyrdin, pleading illness, refused to appear to explain his plans for the crisis.
Some Council members, who are drawn from Russia's regional leaders, called for a motion of no confidence in Chernomyrdin's government and questioned its ability to handle the situation.
Several deputies demanded the government reverse its tight monetary policy and simply print cash to pay wages and pensions.
The Council created another headache for Yeltsin on Thursday when it demanded Ukraine hand over the Black Sea naval port of Sevastopol, saying it was Russia's and Kiev had no right to it.
The move is likely to cause a storm of protest in Ukraine and disrupt delicate negotiations between the two governments.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin would meet Stroyev on Friday.
